tagline: Infographics where the charts come from a table you paste in.
verdictSummary: Piktochart's distinguishing feature against a general design tool is data: paste a table, get a chart already styled to match the poster it sits in. Generating charts from data as SVG is a solved problem with good libraries, and wiring them into a themed vertical layout is a few days. What you are not rebuilding is the template library — the reason people choose Piktochart is that it produces something that looks designed without a designer, and that is a catalogue, not a feature.
coreLoopDIY: Write an infographic as a sequence of themed blocks, paste a CSV into a chart block and get it styled automatically, and export a print-quality poster.
whatYouLose: the template library, which is why the output looks designed
the stock icon and illustration collections
real-time collaboration and brand-kit controls for a team
hosted publishing with a shareable link
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the deliverable has to look professional and most people making an infographic are not designers. A template does that work; a well-built editor does not.
notes: Data-driven charts are the angle, deliberately distinct from the canvas-editor and deck-as-code entries covering the rest of this category.
prompt:
Build an infographic generator where charts are produced from data and styled by a theme.

Document model: a vertical poster of fixed width and variable height, composed of blocks in order. Block types: title, section heading, paragraph, key-figure (a large number with a caption), chart, image, icon row, divider, and a two-column container that can hold two blocks side by side. No free positioning — the layout comes from the block sequence and the theme.

Theme: a token file defining a type scale, a palette with a categorical sequence for charts, spacing, and a background treatment. Every block consumes tokens only, so changing the palette restyles the charts and the text together. Ship two themes and document writing a third.

Charts, which are the point of this build. A chart block takes pasted CSV or TSV, infers column types, and offers only chart types the data can actually support — a bar chart needs one categorical and one numeric column, a line chart needs an ordered dimension, a scatter needs two numerics. Render with Vega-Lite, styled from the theme tokens rather than the library's defaults, so the chart belongs to the poster rather than sitting in it. Support bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, line, area, scatter, and a proportion block (a row of icons or squares representing a percentage, which is the shape infographics actually use most). Refuse pie charts with more than five slices and say why.

Data hygiene, shown rather than hidden: after parsing, display the inferred types and the row count, and flag missing values, duplicated categories and numbers that failed to parse. A chart built silently on a column where a third of the values were text is the failure mode that makes an infographic wrong rather than ugly.

Sources: every chart block carries a source field rendered beneath it in small type, and export refuses to proceed if any chart has an empty source. An infographic without attributions is a rumour.

Export: PNG at a chosen scale, and PDF at print resolution with text kept as text and charts kept as vectors. Warn before export if any block overflows its width or if text falls below a minimum legible size at the export scale.

Storage: the document and its data as JSON on disk, so it lives in a repository and diffs.

Out of scope: a template marketplace, stock illustration libraries, real-time collaboration, hosted publishing, and animated or interactive output.

faq.q: Can I export a Piktochart design?
faq.a: As PNG and PDF, which are final artefacts rather than editable sources. There is no structured export, so a design is rebuilt here — though the data behind the charts usually still exists in whatever spreadsheet it came from, which is the part that matters.

faq.q: Why generate charts rather than let people draw them?
faq.a: Because hand-drawn charts in a design tool are how infographics end up with bars that do not match their numbers. Generating from data means the picture and the figures cannot disagree, and it makes updating a chart a paste rather than a redraw.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing. It runs locally, the chart library is free, and the output is a PNG or PDF file. No account, no server, no keys.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Looking good by default. Piktochart's templates are the product for most of its users, and a well-engineered block editor with two themes will produce something clean and unremarkable. If the infographic exists to impress somebody, that difference is the whole job.
